MR. MARTIN (TIMMINS)  MOTION RESPECTING DOCUMENT PUBLISHED BY SPERRY AND HUTCHINSON COMPANY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege involving this house and all hon. members in it. I have in my possession a document which at first glance appears to be an official report of the debates of this house, but upon examination we find that it is a document put out by the Sperry and Hutchinson Company of Canada Limited. This would lead one to believe that this document was put out by this company with the official sanction of this house.
I might refer to the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1952, volume IV, chapter 274, section 14 of the Unfair Competition Act, which reads as follows:
(1)	No person is entitled to adopt for use in connection with his business, as a trade mark or otherwise, any symbol consisting of, or so nearly resembling as to be likely to be mistaken for-
(e) the arms or crest adopted and used at any time by Canada or by any province or municipal corporation in Canada-
(j) any symbol adopted and used by any public authority in Canada as an official mark on similar wares.
My question of privilege is that this is a direct violation of the statutes and involves a privilege of this house. It was my intention to move that this be referred to the committee on privileges and elections of this house. As that committee has not yet been constituted I move, seconded by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier):
That the president of the Sperry and Hutchinson Company of Canada Limited be ordered to attend at the bar of this house on the 18th day of February, 1960 at 2.30 p.m.

subtopic: CIVIL SERVICE COMMISSION REPORT ON PAY INCREASES, 1959

Motion No. 2-Mr. Mcllrailh:

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: CIVIL SERVICE COMMISSION REPORT ON PAY INCREASES, 1959
speechtext:
Hon. members will recall that when this motion came before the house on February 3 a point of order was raised by the hon. member for Ottawa West which I undertook to take into consideration. Upon looking into the matter I found that a point of procedure arose as to the form of motion for obtaining the production of documents, and I thought it better to put down my conclusions in writing, which I shall now give to the house.
When this notice of motion was read on Wednesday, February 3, Hansard pages 684 to 686, the Minister of Finance stated that the report in question was confidential, having been made in pursuance of the Civil Service

Motions for Papers
Act by the civil service commission to the government and to the Minister of Finance. The hon. member for Ottawa West raised a point of order, that the right of the minister to object to the tabling of such a document was limited to such documents under his administrative responsibility and did not extend to reports of this kind made by the civil service commission, an independent body answerable to parliament and not to the government of the day. The hon. member for Ottawa West and the house were good enough to allow the motion to stand to give me an opportunity to consider the point which he had raised. The Minister of Justice reminded the house of the provisions of standing order 47 which permits such a motion, if a debate on it is desired, to be transferred by the Clerk to the order of notices of motion, thereby suggesting, as I understood him, that the point raised by the hon. member for Ottawa West was a point of debate rather than a point of order.
In view of what I am about to express it is perhaps unnecessary to determine whether the hon. member for Ottawa West properly raised his objection as a point of order. There have been such discussions before. On April 3, 1957, pages 3007 to 3015 of Hansard, there was a long discussion as on points of order on the practice which the house would expect the minister to follow in indicating his unwillingness to accept a motion for papers under his control.
I have come to the conclusion that whatever ruling I might make as to the right of the Minister of Finance to oppose the production of the report in question, the house will have to decide by its vote whether or not the document is to be produced, unless of course the motion is withdrawn, as often happens when production is objected to. I repeat that it is for the house to decide after debate, if desired, whether it will or will not order that the document in question be laid on the table.
This will be so whether or not I uphold the contention of the hon. member for Ottawa West. It would be quite improper for the Speaker to substitute his decision for that of the house, and his jurisdiction does not extend to constitutional questions, questions of law or other matters which are for the determination of the house itself. I refer hon. members to Beauchesne's fourth edition, page 180, citation 71, paragraph 5.
However, it is my responsibility to see that the motion is before the house in the proper form, that is whether or not it is the appropriate motion to do what is sought to be done. As I have come to the conclusion

that it is not, I think 1 should state briefly the principles that apply to such motions for the production of papers.
As it is well known, papers are laid before the house in pursuance of (1) provisions of an act of parliament; (2) an order of the house itself; (3) an address to the crown; (4) the command of the crown; (5) the standing orders of the house. The reference for that statement is Beauchesne's fourth edition, page 176, citation 209.
There are two annual reports which are to be made to parliament under the Civil Service Act. One is under subsection 4 of section 4, which reads as follows:
(4) The commission shall make an annual report and statement of the transactions and affairs of the commission during the year then next preceding, and the report shall he laid before parliament.
The other report to parliament is made pursuant to subsection 2 of section 60, which gives the commission power with the approval of the governor in council to exclude certain positions from the operations of the act and to make regulations dealing with such positions. Subsection 2 of section 60 reads in part as follows:
(2)	The commission shall make an annual report to parliament within thirty days from the commencement of each session setting forth the positions excluded under this section-
And so on. The document asked for in this case is not either of these annual reports to be laid before parliament, but if I understand the motion correctly it is the report referred to in section 11 of the Civil Service Act, which reads as follows:
11. (1) The commission shall, from time to time, as may be necessary, recommend rates of compensation for any new classes that may be established hereunder, and may propose changes in the rates of compensation for existing classes.
(2)	In each class there shall be a minimum and a maximum salary rate and such intermediate rates as may be considered necessary and proper to provide increases between the minimum and maximum.
(3)	Proposed rates of compensation shall become operative only upon their approval by the governor in council, and, where any increased expenditure will result therefrom, when parliament has provided the money required for such increased expenditure.
That is the whole of section 11. If, to use the words of the motion, the "report made to the Minister of Finance in the year 1959 by the civil service commission concerning pay increases for civil servants" is made under this section, how should it be asked for having regard to the fact that the civil service commission is not part of the administrative responsibility of the Minister of Finance or of the department, I may say, over which he presides? In this matter the hon. member for Ottawa West is correct, and the recommended

rates of compensation become operative only upon their approval by the governor in council.
Beauchesne, in citation 209, sets out this procedure, and I think I might take a minute in order to refer to it. He deals with orders for the production of papers, and he says this in citation 209, page 176 of the fourth edition:
(2)	Papers may be directly ordered when they relate to-
And I leave out the intervening words.
-matters under the immediate control and direction of the different departments of the dominion-
That is the case with an order for the production of documents. Then as to addresses as distinguished from orders:
(3)	Addresses are moved for papers and dispatches from the imperial government; for orders in council.. . for petitions and memorials not in the possession of the House but addressed to the governor in council-
A little further down he continues:
The general rule is that information to be obtained from or through any department constituted or regulated by statute, is obtained by means of an order, whilst information to be obtained from or through the privy council, is obtained by means of an address.
May has an explanation in somewhat similar terms of the practice in the parliament of the United Kingdom which I should like to quote briefly. I am quoting from May's sixteenth edition at page 270:
Parliament is invested with the power of ordering all documents to be laid before it, which are necessary for its information. Each house enjoys this authority separately, but not in all cases independently of the crown. Accounts and papers relating to trade, finance, and general or local matters, are ordered directly, and are returned in obedience to the order of the house whence it was issued: but returns of matters connected with the exercise of the royal prerogative, are obtained by means of addresses to the crown.
The distinction between these two classes of returns should be borne in mind: as, on the one hand, it is irregular to order directly that which should be sought for by address; and, on the order, it is a compromise of the authority of parliament to resort to the crown for information which it can obtain by its own order.
It is clear, I think, from these authorities that the information to be obtained from or through the crown is obtained by means of an address. If we agree that the recommendations of the civil service commission pursuant to section 11 of the Civil Service Act are to be submitted to the governor in council and that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) is only the vehicle, this document is now officially in the possession of the governor in council and should be asked for from that source.
That being so, I am of the opinion that the motion by the hon. member for Ottawa West should not have been drafted as an 79951-0-67
Division
order of the house to issue these documents, but that it should have been drafted in the form of an address which it is usual to prepare in the following terms:
-that an humble address be presented to His Excellency the Governor General praying that he will cause to be laid before the house a copy-
Then follows whatever document is desired.
However, this is a matter of form only which it is simple to correct. If the hon. member for Ottawa West will agree to substituting the appropriate motion for an address for the present motion for an order I shall be pleased to make the correction and the matter can be proceeded with. I understand that the hon. member agrees to this.

maintopic: PROPOSED EXTENSION OF BENEFITS TO CANADIAN WOODSMEN IN STATE OF MAINE
PROPOSED EXTENSION OF BENEFITS TO CANADIAN WOODSMEN IN STATE OF MAINE
speechtext:
That in the opinion of this house the government should consider the advisability of discussing with the appropriate United States authorities the question of unemployment insurance benefits to Canadian woodsmen working in the state of Maine.
(Translation):
He said: Mr. Speaker, I submitted this resolution following numerous requests from bushworkers who go out to work in the United States and complained to me that under those conditions, they were unable to receive unemployment insurance benefits.
(Text):

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: PROPOSED EXTENSION OF BENEFITS TO CANADIAN WOODSMEN IN STATE OF MAINE
speechtext:
Order. I wonder if the hon. member would pause for a minute to give members leaving the house an opportunity to go, while I ask others to observe silence so we may hear the hon. member for Beauce.
(Translation):

maintopic: PROPOSED EXTENSION OF BENEFITS TO CANADIAN WOODSMEN IN STATE OF MAINE
speechtext:
On March 6 and 12, 1952, the Canadian government and the United States government signed an agreement for the protection, from an unemployment point of view, of Canadian workers in the United States and American labour in Canada. The agreement had favourable results, for indeed, today, workers of both countries enjoy adequate protection anywhere in Canada and with our neighbours to the south, except in the states of Iowa, Maine, New Hampshire and Alabama.
From an economic point of view, the proximity to the United States of a certain area of Quebec and part of New Brunswick makes it possible, each year, for quite a few Canadians to find jobs over there in the lumber industry. In fact because of this proximity to Maine, New Hampshire, and the states of New York and Vermont, permission was obtained from the American immigration department for 9,000 of our fellow citizens to find employment with our neighbours in 1959.
The workers get employment in those states and temporarily immigrate in either of two ways: for instance the worker can enter the United States with a six month pass, and is restricted to specific employment; or else the workers cross the border after obtaining a visa which authorizes them to do so at will

Unemployment Insurance
and to change jobs as they like. The latter group comprises 1,500 people.
According to the reports submitted by the director of unemployment insurance at a meeting held in Boston on December 22, 1959, the monthly average number of Canadians working in American industries during the three years preceding 1959, was as follows: from September 1956 to August 1957, 5,256 men; from September 1957 to August 1958, 2,780 men; from September 1958 to March 1959, 2,343 men.
About 70 per cent of those people go to Maine, and are employed in lumber camps there in a proportion of 70 per cent; the others are engaged in service operations.
We note that in the last few years, the monthly average number of Canadian workers taking jobs in the United States has declined considerably.
The greatest number of jobs available to Canadians is in Maine, and and, of course, in a lesser proportion, in the state of New Hampshire. The proportion is also less significant in the states of New York and Vermont. But, as far as those two states are concerned, there is noting amiss, as mutual agreements have been signed in both cases.
The fact remains that Maine and New Hampshire absorb practically all our bush-workers but as those states have no agreement with Canada, our men are less interested in working in those two states, because they cannot count on adequate protection in case of unemployment when they return to Canada.
Therefore, those Canadians, working in states where there is no mutual agreement, cannot qualify for benefits when they are unemployed. Though the states concerned and Canada have each their own legislation, those men cannot qualify in Canada because they do not pay enough contributions here to qualify under our own legislation.
And in the absence of a reciprocity agreement, they are likewise barred from benefits in the United States, because they live in Canada and are not residents of the state in which they are employed.
In proposing this resolution asking that steps be taken, in order to find some solution to the problem I have no intention of casting blame on anybody.
I know that for several years now discussions have been held between Canadian government authorities and representatives from Maine and New Hampshire.
In addition to those discussions, I know that there has been an exchange of correspondence between unemployment commission officers and members of a similar commission in Maine and New Hampshire.

I would not like this resolution to be interpreted today as a blame-as I said-for its main purpose is to urge the Minister of Labour and commission members to activate their discussions to determine whether it is possible to come to an agreement.
After so many years of discussions, I believe it would be desirable, in the interest of those workers, that we know exactly whether it is possible or not.
I know that those two states raise certain objections to reciprocity, because first of all, they feel that, under the circumstances, Canadians would be getting much more from the state funds than American workers would get out of Canadian funds.
In the report submitted to the meeting of October 23 in Boston, special mention was made of the fact that the balance of requests and applications in the 17 years the reciprocal agreement has been established, had been about the same; but in both states concerned it is readily understood that it is very likely, and even possible, that applications come mostly from Canadians.
In the second place, American employers fear that, in view of the ease with which Canadians are allowed to cross the border, once those workers come back to Canada, U. S. employers would not have the same opportunity of hiring them once the men apply for unemployment insurance. Employers claim they have a better opportunity to rehire American citizens. Furthermore, they fear that since Canadian workers are paid by the U. S. government unemployment commission, they would not perhaps be as eager to take certain jobs for which they would be required in the United States.
As a result of those various reasons, American employers fear that their preferential rates, according to their experience, would be heavily increased.
Third, the authorities of the states concerned and employers fear that Canadians may not be so readily available, that is to say that the law may not be applied in Canada as strictly as it is now in the United States, and that it is rather difficult to establish such availability, through Canadian unemployment insurance offices.
Those are the main reasons given by our American neighbours for not agreeing to the reciprocal agreement.
However, I feel that-even if nothing was said about that during the discussions-what those two states fear most is that Canadian employees get too much out of Maine and New Hampshire funds and that, in return, reciprocity, in the above-mentioned case, would be detrimental to them, since very few Americans have jobs in that part of Quebec and New Brunswick and that, consequently,

they would be called upon to pay much more in benefits than the Canadian unemployment insurance fund would have to pay to American citizens.
Consequently, under the circumstances, it would be necessary to determine whether or not the day will come when an agreement will be possible.
If none is possible, it is the duty of the Canadian government and of the unemployment insurance commission authorities to find solutions in case it would be absolutely impossible to come to a reciprocal agreement such as already exists between Canada and other states of the neighbouring country.
If reciprocal insurability is impossible, Canadian authorities should come up with suggestions to protect those jobs for our citizens in the United States.
Not only must those relations be encouraged, but it is our duty to safeguard them, and also, through appropriate measures, to encourage Canadian citizens to keep those jobs which, in the circumstances, considerably help reduce unemployment in this country.
If our woods workers were to lose interest altogether in the jobs they can get in the United States, as a result of lack of protection in case of unemployment, those people would only swell the already long list of unemployed in Canada, which is quite impressive.
If the discussions between Maine, New Hampshire and Canada have had little success, I think the officials of the Department of Labour, jointly with the unemployment commission authorities should consider other solutions, because much of the responsibility for the welfare of those Canadian workers who earn their living in the United States, and spend their income in Canada, lies in the hands of Canadian authorities.
Besides, that is the opinion entertained, and rightly so, by members of the regional employment advisory committee of my constituency, as recorded in the minutes of their meeting held in St. Georges, on October 29, 1959, and I quote:
Members are of the opinion that it is within the unemployment commission itself that the problem should be solved. One must not overlook the fact that those citizens are 100 per cent Canadians, that they spend up to 99 per cent of their income in Canada, that they pay taxes like all other woods workers employed in Canada. Consequently, it is the duty of the unemployment insurance commission to hasten the solution of that problem. The unemployment insurance commission can, with the agreement of the governor in council, make rules to include under insurable employment, any job partly
Unemployment Insurance or fully done outside Canada, if such job would be insurable if performed in Canada. Let then the commission introduce some regulation, accordingly, for the benefit of Canadian bush workers working in Maine and New Hampshire, restricting, however, the insurability to those who work over there for Canadian contractors, operating in both states concerned. Check ups could be simplified by duplicate statements of salaries paid to those bushworkers, which statements could be kept on file at employers' offices in Canadian territory. That a copy of this resolution be forwarded to the federal Minister of Labour, to the chief commissioner of the unemployment insurance commission and to the member for Beauce in the House of Commons.
The commission might oppose this resolution. First of all, it will surely be said that the agreement, in the circumstances, would be limited to Canadian employers and contractors having their place of business in Canada; second, it might also be said that such an agreement would be more or less non-compulsory and that some contractors could take part in it or not, since Maine legislation would still apply to those bush-workers.
Furthermore, it will be said that the state of Maine has not the power to withdraw its present tax, and that the Canadian contractor would find himself handicapped compared to his American competitors, in view of his contributions to the U.S. treasury and to the Canadian unemployment insurance fund.
It will also be said that non-compulsory participation might create an anomaly, in view of the fact that some woodsworkers would be protected while others would not, something which might cause a good deal of discontent.
It may also be added that employers, to avoid double taxation, would be inclined to hire American workers rather than Canadians, something which would spoil the employment market for Canadians.
Under the circumstances, it may be said that this resolution would, in the long run, do more harm than good from the particular point of view of employment.
I think that, sooner or later, this motion will have to be given serious consideration, in view of the fact that discussions between Canada and the state of Maine have so far shown little progress. So naturally, the commission, in co-operation with the Department of Labour, will have to give more serious consideration to this proposal in order to reach a compromise aimed at helping and protecting Canadian workers.
If we insist on going on with the discussions with the state of Maine, without taking note

Unemployment Insurance of suggestions from various organizations, I think our workers will have to wait another several years, and even at that, will not be assured of satisfactory results, assuming that an agreement is finally reached after a number of years.
Perhaps the commission should, in cooperation with the Department of Labour, make an objective study of proposals that are being submitted and not only discover their weak points, if any, but it is the responsibility of the Department of Labour and of the unemployment insurance commission to try to find a way out.
I have no wish to criticize the Department of Labour or the unemployment insurance commission authorities, but in view of their lack of success and results so far in reciprocal discussions with the states concerned, I think instead of raising objections against plans that are submitted, they should look for solutions and formulas to protect that employment market, which is one of the most important markets for the area extending from Sherbrooke to New Brunswick. Let them negotiate a solution, if not with the state of Maine, at least with employers who need the services of Canadian workers.
I have every reason to believe that American employers in forestry operations are quite favourably disposed toward Canadian citizens who work for them at certain periods of the year, and I urge the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) to get in touch with the largest companies employing Canadians for a good part of the year in their forestry operations.
I have no wish to commit those American employers in any way, but though I am in no position to say officially that they are willing to co-operate, I can at least say it unofficially, because I know they want to keep their Canadian workers for their operations. Therefore, perhaps it might be advisable to have discussions with them, because I think the problem of double taxation might easily be settled. I am certain that American lumbering companies might be, under the circumstances, not only interested but prepared to show their co-operation by assuming, on the one hand, most of the costs with regard to American taxation, as far as the employee and the employer are concerned, I am also convinced that they would not be disinclined to have a representative in Canada to look after the bookkeeping in respect of salaries so that the

unemployment insurance commission might, in due course, check the wages of our Canadian workers employed in the United States. In this way, all our workers would be protected without any exception or discrimination.
Thus, it would be quite easy for unemployment insurance commission auditors to go to the Canadian office of those companies and check the case of such and such employee who applies for unemployment insurance.
As I said just now, the government and the Department of Labour-and I agree with them-have had negotiations with the states of Maine and New Hampshire only. But after all this time we will agree that we take other steps and change our policy, because I am convinced that, before long, if things keep up this way and if we neither come to a better arrangement nor reach more appreciable results with regard to safeguarding our economy on that employment market, and giving our workers some economic and social guarantee, I am certain, that in a not too remote future, we shall have to face the loss of that employment market because our lumbermen and bushworkers will have to face problems which, at this time, they are unable to solve. They will prefer trying to get jobs in Quebec or Ontario, rather than to go out to the United States and have no guarantee of being able to get unemployment insurance benefits on their return to Canada.
In the statistics I mentioned a few moments ago and which were quoted by the unemployment insurance administrators at the Boston meeting, on September 22, 1959, we notice that, since 1956, the number of our Canadian workers engaged in American lumber operations, had decreased by half as of March 1959, and I am afraid that, if the government does not consider the possibility of new negotiations with the employers, the number of men who are now finding jobs in the United States, will decline in the same proportion within a few years and that, in the near future, we will witness the loss of that labour market which I consider most important, because, a few years ago, some
20,000	men from those areas of Quebec and New Brunswick found employment there.
That question has often been raised in the house before, and representations have been made. I remember finding in Hansard that the former member for Compton-Frontenac (Mr. Blanchette), the former member for Dor-

Chester, the member for Bellechasse, and also my immediate predecessor from Beauce raised the question in many of their speeches.
I remember seeing in Hansard of former years that the matter was also dealt with by the hon. member for Restigouche-Mada-waska (Mr. Van Horne), whom I am pleased to see in the house today, and who, I am sure, will give us his comments and suggestions about this problem.
Mr. Speaker, I particularly want to say that this question does not apply exclusively to Beauce constituency, nor to Dorchester and Compton-Frontenac constituencies, but to all the area extending from Sherbrooke to New Brunswick and especially to many local unemployment insurance offices, including, among others, St. Georges, Sherbrooke, Me-gantic, Riviere du Loup, Montmagny, Cau-sapscal, Matane, Campbellton and Fredericton. The offices deal with workers who are now handicapped by this "no agreement restriction" between Maine and New Hampshire and Canada.
Consequently, it is not a matter of purely local interest since it affects two provinces, and I hope that the minister as well as the officials of the unemployment insurance commission will continue to give it special consideration.
Before concluding, may I offer, on behalf of those workers, my most sincere congratulation to the former minister of labour, Mr. Gregg, and to the present minister who have both worked so hard in taking up this matter with the states of Maine and New Hampshire. May I also congratulate the unemployment insurance commission officials who, in many circumstances, spared no effort in trying to bring about an agreement between Maine and New Hampshire. However, the Minister of Labour and the officials of the unemployment insurance commission should not be satisfied with the congratulations I have offered them and I hope that after their involuntary failure to bring about a mutual agreement, they will give consideration to the resolutions that have been suggested to them so that this problem, that I consider most important, may be settled soon.
I hope also that during this debate many solutions will be suggested by the members of the house. In fact, I hope that the members for Compton-Frontenac, Dorchester, Bellechasse and Montmagny-L'Islet, as well as the members from Gaspesia and New Brunswick 79951-0-68
Unemployment Insurance will share in this debate in a constructive way in order to help the Minister of Labour and the unemployment insurance commission find a solution to this problem, and in this way help all our woodsmen who are employed in the United States, and particularly in the two states which do not have an agreement with Canada.
Besides, here is what I find in the insurance coverage manual:
That the commission may, with the approval of the governor in council, make regulations to include in insurable employment any job outside Canada which, if it were done in Canada, would be insurable employment.
Sections C-301 to C-304 inclusive deal with seamen.
Section C-305 deals with other jobs outside Canada and it read as follows:
(1)	Regulation 66 passed under section 66 (1)
(b)	of the act gives coverage to: employment for the execution of any particular work done by a person who was insured before his departure from Canada, for an employer residing in or having a place of Dusiness in Canada. Unless the com mission decides otherwise in a particular case, this rule normally applies only to the job which must not last more than eight months.
(2)	Ordinary considerations governing the insurability of an occupation apply naturally to occupations outside Canada listed above in paragraph (1), but those occupations must also meet the following requirements:
(a)	the worker must have been insured just before leaving Canada:
(b)	the occupation must involve "the performance of specific duties";
(c)	the insured person must have been employed before leaving Canada or, if this person is already out of Canada, employment or re-employment must uninterruptedly follow a previous employment outside of Canada, for which contributions were required;
(d)	the employer must reside in Canada or have a place of business in this country.
This resolution does not by any means purport to put an end to talks with the states of Maine and New Hampshire. But since talks held up to now have obviously proved unsuccessful, I ask the Minister of Labour to carry them on while opening new negotiations with American employers, who seem very well disposed, because I think this problem should be settled within the unemployment insurance commission.
Therefore, I think a solution to this situation could be found in section 305, if the companies agree to send representatives to Canada, whether they be contractors, subcontractors or others. In this way Canadian woodsmen employed in Maine or New Hampshire could pay unemployment insurance contributions and qualify for benefits during slack

Unemployment Insurance periods. This would help to maintain their interest in seeking employment south of the border, thus creating employment for other Canadians who are now out of work.

maintopic: PROPOSED EXTENSION OF BENEFITS TO CANADIAN WOODSMEN IN STATE OF MAINE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the subject matter of this resolution interests me very much. I heartily commend the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Racine) for bringing this matter to the attention of parliament and the public in general because it is a matter which I feel is not too well understood.
I congratulate the hon. member on the remarks he made although it was rather difficult for me to hear him at all times and to hear the translation. I believe the hon. gentleman was fair in his presentation but that he strayed somewhat from the subject of the resolution. When I read the resolution I considered it somewhat misleading in that the hon. gentleman appeared to be asking the government to take action. The inference to be drawn from the resolution was that the government had done nothing in this respect and this attitude, of course, is most unfair. In general, however, the hon. member covered the subject fairly thoroughly.
It is not my intention to read the resolution because hon. gentlemen have it before them. I have been interested in the problem dealt with in the resolution for a period of six years. This problem was brought to my attention shortly after I became a member of parliament because there are many people in my constituency and in the area to the north of it as well as in other parts of New Brunswick who like to go to the state of Maine and work in the lumber industry. One reason is because the wages are greater.
The lumber business in the states of Maine, New Hampshire and throughout the eastern United States follows a pattern similar to that prevalent in eastern Canada. The industry has problems and fluctuations. These fluctuations result in many of these workers being laid off for periods extending between two and four months during the year. These men about whom we are speaking wish to maintain their residence in Canada but like to go across the border and work in the lumber industry- chiefly in the paper industry-and then, when laid off, return to Canada. I first took up the matter with the former minister of labour in 1954 who told me there were several hon.


members in that parliament interested in the question.
As a result of the agreement which the hon. member for Beauce mentioned in his remarks which went into effect April 12, 1942 negotiations were entered into between Canada and several states and some were successfully concluded. In 1954 negotiations were undertaken with the state of Maine to see what could be done. It was found that the wood operators who are the employers of these men were not interested and would in no way support the arranging of a reciprocal agreement. That attitude has continued to the present day.
The effect of the agreements entered into in 1942 between Canada and the United States was to permit agencies in either country to undertake reciprocal arrangements. The interpretation of that is that the unemployment insurance commission in Canada has the right and authority to enter into an agreement with the state employment security commission of any state in the United States concerning unemployment benefits. However, no headway could be made with the authorities in the state of Maine.
I shall outline the discussions I had on the matter with the former minister of labour. In 1954, as I said, the government of the day attempted to reach an agreement with the state of Maine but nothing was done. As a result of meetings held at that time the employment security commission authorities of the state of Maine said in effect that their employers were not interested in and would not support a reciprocal arrangement and therefore the state of Maine would not enter into an agreement. They expressed their position in plain cold words.
Nothing further was done until about 1956. I was one of several hon. members of that parliament who discussed this question with the then minister of labour who assured us that his departmental officials would again take up the matter through Washington. If I remember correctly this matter was referred to the labour councillor who discussed it with his opposite number. He came back with the information that there had been efforts made by the labour councillor and the director of the bureau of employment security in Washington to initiate proposals in congress for reciprocal coverage by the states with Canada.
However, there was no success because they immediately ran into political repercussions on state rights. This was in 1956, and we seemed to be up against a stone wall.
Then, when the present Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr), came into office various hon. members of parliament got after him and his

departmental officials and directed him to press the matter much more strenuously and actively. He even took it up with the governors of Maine and New Hampshire. The letters which were produced last year show that he urged the governor of Maine to take action, and they also show that the governor referred the matter to the state employment security commission. Later our minister received information that the state was not interested. The minister also referred the problem to Governor Muskie's successor, who seems to be favourably inclined to do what he can. The matter rests there at the moment.
This question was also referred to Governor Dwinell of New Hampshire. This is something which I believe should be brought to the attention of all hon. members of this house. This is an international matter. The governor of New Hampshire informed our Department of Labour that in so far as the state of New Hampshire was concerned the state employment security commission had no authority to enter into an agreement until their legislature amends this statutory law. Now, as I say, this was discovered late in 1957 by our present Minister of Labour.
I should like to read a paragraph from Governor Dwinell's letter which is pertinent. This letter was among the papers tabled last spring. I am quoting now from a letter written by Lane Dwinell, governor of the state of New Hampshire, to the Hon. Michael Starr, Minister of Labour, dated December 31, 1957.
As to the possibility of entering into a reciprocal agreement, it is my understanding that under the present state of the law relating to employment security in my state no such agreement can be made. The language relating to such arrangements is revised statutes annotated of New Hampshire, chapter 282, section 16-A, "The director of the division of employment security is hereby authorized to enter into reciprocal arrangements with appropriate and duly authorized agencies of other states or of the federal government, or both-[DOT]
The interpretation of the word "state" is this:
-"State" includes, in addition to the states of the United States of America, Alaska, Hawaii, and the District of Columbia.
So far as the state of New Hampshire is concerned, to which a lot of our woodsmen seem to like to go to work, until the legislators of New Hampshire are ready to change the law we just cannot force them to do so.
The minister and his departmental officials did not stop there. During the last three years they have interested the international brotherhood of pulp, sulphite and papermill workers and that organization has taken up the case in New Hampshire and Maine. They have taken up the case on behalf of the Canadian woodsmen. However, even with the assistance of this organization there has been 79951-0-684
Unemployment Insurance no success in getting this statute changed in New Hampshire. There is very little that our Department of Labour can do because these people have no authority whatever to enter into an agreement.
I believe that the solution of this problem lies pretty well within the hands of Canadian labour. As the hon. member who spoke before me said, I believe that Canadian woodsmen are the best. It is my opinion that the pulp and paper operators in both the state of Maine and New Hampshire are anxious to retain these men as employees. It was suggested, I believe in some of the correspondence, by one of the governors of one of the states that Canada might refuse these labourers permission to go to work in the United States. We do not want to do that. I do not believe any member of the house would ask the government to do that. However, if labourers refused to go over there to work, then the operators might take a different attitude.
As a matter of fact, if I remember correctly this matter was thoroughly discussed at a meeting of the pulp and paper operators held in Boston last May. It was suggested at that time that they might run into difficulty in getting Canadian woodsmen unless some provision was made for unemployment insurance coverage by the states of Maine and New Hampshire. Of course, the operators have not come up against this situation as yet, but the problem was serious enough, I am informed, to necessitate a further meeting being called in September. I think the hon. member referred to that matter but I could not catch just what he said there.
Representatives of the state employment security commission in the states of Maine and New Hampshire were there, as were representatives of the operators of the pulp and paper industry and, I believe, on invitation, representatives of the unemployment insurance commission of Canada. The matter was thoroughly discussed but without concrete results. However, as a result of that meeting I think the operators feel that they may have to do something. They would have to do something if the Canadian woodsmen refuse to go there and work.
I agree with the hon. member who spoke ahead of me that we do not want to lose that labour market if we can help it. But when we are dealing with an international matter like this, it is necessary to use pressure. From the information I can gather on this whole subject-and I have followed it closely since 1954-I do not think at any time has the department and the officials of the minister pressed more consistently and more actively in this matter than did our present Minister of Labour and his officials during
1068	HOUSE OF
Unemployment Insurance the last two years. If he had not been putting the pressure on, I do not think we would have had that meeting which was held in September and which, to my mind, is possibly going to bring some results provided the Canadian woodsmen will stick their heels in and refuse to go there and work unless some arrangement is made.
The Canadian government and the Department of Labour cannot make any trade with the lumber operators in either the state of Maine or the state of New Hampshire unless there is an arrangement whereby deposits are made in Canada and they are backed up by these men refusing to go there and work. With the pressure being kept up, with the discussions that have been taking place being continued and with the support of our own Canadian workmen I believe that we could be successful in getting some sort of reciprocal agreement.
As the former hon. member I think said- I am not too sure about this, but I think he did so-these operators have been opposing this reciprocal agreement because it would mean they would be obliged to contribute more tax to the security commission of each state. However, I think they would be willing to do that in order to get our Canadian woodsmen. That is the impression I gather as a result of the meetings that have been held.
I did not like the resolution in the beginning but it has possibly had the effect of bringing to the attention of the public the fact that we have today a Minister of Labour who has been doing everything he can to bring this matter to a head. When I say that I am not making any reflection on the former minister of labour. He was a personal friend of mine. I discussed this matter with him on various occasions; and I was not the only one to do so. However, they never seemed to be successful.
They never seemed to be able to get that union interested in lobbying as they are getting interested now, something which I think is a good thing. They never approached Washington in order to try to have this thing forced through. What was the use? You cannot force a foreign government to do something in a matter like that; you must encourage them. I think we have the matter in our hands. If our Canadian workmen stick in their heels I think we can win the operators over. I think we must insist that our department continue this same pressure they have been putting on. However, I cannot agree at the moment that we should pay.
Maybe I have misunderstood the hon. member on this matter. I cannot see that we should pay these people unemployment insurance out of the Canadian unemployment


insurance fund in any circumstances unless we can get contributions from the state of Maine or from the log operators. On that point I may be wrong. As I say, I may have misunderstood my hon. friend. However, I cannot go along with that argument. I would be against it.
Another thing I should like to point out is this. My impression is that a debate like this in the house is a good thing because it informs the public of what has been done. There are a good many people in my province-and they are not only woodsmen- who think the government has not done anything in the last ten years. They will hardly believe you when you tell them the government has been working on this matter at least since 1954. I think this debate is good for that purpose. At first I felt that a resolution like this should not be debated for the purpose of trying to give the impression the government was not doing anything whereas they were doing all they could. However, I know that was not the intention of the hon. member. As a result of this debate I think the public will become informed of what the government is trying to do and possibly that fact will be of some help.
I think I have said about all I wish to say on this matter. However, in conclusion I should like to say this even at the risk of repeating myself. I think the minister and his officials in the Department of Labour are to be commended for their active and persistent action in this matter. I think it is a good thing to let the public know that they have been forcing this issue through. We may get more support from the public and the people particularly interested.
From what I have read of the correspondence that has been tabled, I think the governors of these two states are sympathetic. I think the trouble in the past has lain in the fact that the operators objected. As a result of this meeting in September I am a little bit more hopeful.
Just in closing I should like to say this. I am sure that we could not get a more dedicated man to follow up this matter than our own Minister of Labour today. I wish him every success as I am sure does every hon. member in the house who is interested in this matter. It is rather hard to compel a foreign government-and that is what we are dealing with, really-to do something unless we have some lever. We have it, of course, if our workmen work with us. I will say this. If the minister does not succeed, it will not be for lack of trying.

maintopic: PROPOSED EXTENSION OF BENEFITS TO CANADIAN WOODSMEN IN STATE OF MAINE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member tor Beauce (Mr. Racine) has introduced a most interesting and important resolution. In its own wording it is very restrictive because it deals wholly and solely with the matter of woodsmen. However, we feel that the vital importance of the motion is that it brings to the notice of this parliament a factor or a matter that has not been considered too fully in the past and which, without any question of doubt at all, requires the consideration of the federal government and the provincial governments of this country and the national government and the state governments of the country to the south.
We have over 3,000 miles of border between Canada and the United States, and especially on a season basis there is a transfer from south to north, but particularly from north to south, as regards work. It is for that reason we feel that the hon. member has done something to draw to the attention of this government and the hon. members of this house the need for over-all planning and policy and international understanding with regard to transference of workers from one country to the other.
The previous speaker said he was not going to read the motion but, sir, I am, and you will understand in a moment why. The motion is as follows:
That in the opinion of this house the government should consider the advisability of discussing with the appropriate United States authorities the question of unemployment insurance benefits to Canadian woodsmen working in the state of Maine.
As I said a moment ago, it is directed toward Canadian woodsmen working in one state of the United States. I have already mentioned the over-all picture internationally, which I feel is the larger aspect which is opened up by this motion, but basically I am afraid that what I have to say is more in the way of seeking information than being by way of comment.
I regret a great deal that neither the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) nor the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) is here; because there are very far-reaching implications in even the specific matter mentioned in the motion. We in this party are most interested in the motion and have made some study of the Unemployment Insurance Act to see how it is affected. I listened with a great deal of interest on the simultaneous translation system to the remarks of the mover of the motion. We have also noted points in the existing act with regard to the application of unemployment insurance if a Canadian worker crosses the border and works in the United States.
Unemployment Insurance
Our interpretation of the existing power of the unemployment insurance commission, and that also means the existing power of the Minister of Labour, is that there can only be negotiation, as far as United States employers paying unemployment insurance contributions for a Canadian workman is concerned, if the Canadian workman is employed prior to going to the United States in a certain occupation for a certain employer and he works for that same employer in the United States. If I am wrong about that I most certainly would like some clarification; but it is my understanding that even if this idea were carried through, good as it is, no arrangement could be made because under the Unemployment Insurance Act of Canada the unemployment insurance commission and the Minister of Labour have no authority to make any agreement with a state in the United States, or with Washington itself, for the payment of unemployment insurance on a Canadian basis for a Canadian working wholly and solely for a United States employer in the United States.
It was for that reason that I said that although we are most interested in this motion-we think it is most important and hope something can be worked out-would we not first of all have to have an amendment to our own Unemployment Insurance Act so as to give the authority to make some international agreement, or agreement between a province and a state, whereby a United States employer employing a Canadian worker could pay a contribution for unemployment insurance in Canada? That is the first angle on which I would like some clarification. If my interpretation is wrong, I hope I am very hurriedly corrected.
In addition, Mr. Speaker-perhaps this is even a more important point, although quite honestly I have not yet resolved it myself- the implications of this matter are so vital. We can understand the principle. There must be thousands of Canadians who cross the border to an adjoining state on a seasonal basis to go to work. The hon. member who moved the motion told us of the thousands of woodsmen in his own province and constituency who go down into the state of Maine. From my discussions with other hon. members of all parties in the house, there are thousands more outside of woodsmen, such as those who dig potatoes and pick apples. I understand the figure runs into thousands in the province of Quebec and some of the maritime provinces. Of course, they are not covered by unemployment insurance in Canada, and they could not be covered to any extent in their employment in the United States. There is not much we can do about
1070	HOUSE OF
Unemployment Insurance that until we correct the situation in Canada, but I would like to cover the implications of this principle.
I hope it can be shown as good, but would it not be the fact that if we amended our own Unemployment Insurance Act to give the unemployment insurance commission or the Minister of Labour the authority to try to negotiate with Washington or with the state concerned where a Canadian workman working for a United States employer in the United States for three, four or five months pays unemployment insurance, the employer's payment is then applicable for unemployment in Canada? If that is so, and if that is good, then does it therefore follow that where a United States citizen is working in Canada, or a Mexican or Venezuelan is working in Canada on, say, oil, we would agree to pay to those countries payments of unemployment insurance if they have such a thing, or workmen's compensation, or whatever it is? Or do we maintain what we do at present, and that is that anyone coming into our country is covered by our law? As far as I understand it, they are covered under our law.
Of course, the laws in the United States with regard to compensation are entirely different from ours. If we establish this principle, does that mean that our workmen in the United States^-and I would say that the woodsmen follow a most dangerous occupation-are covered under the compensation laws of the United States, or Canada? If they are covered by unemployment insurance in Canada, then are they covered by workmen's compensation in Canada and, if so, is the employer going to pay the workmen's compensation in Canada? Or is it the case that they stand by what they have? It varies from state to state, I understand. In some places everything is covered by insurance, and not by the kind of system we have in Canada. That is a point very much in my mind, and it is raised because of the principle espoused here.
It is also my understanding that the woodsmen who go from the riding of the hon. member who moved this resolution into the state of Maine have paid for them by their employers the social security tax. They pay the social security tax of the United States. What is the position of the Canadian woodsmen from the hon. member's riding who go to Maine and whose employers are now paying the social security tax which the law of the state says they have to pay? Is there any return to the 'Canadians when they are back in their own home country? I am told that if you work in the United States for so many years you reach a certain point, and then it 

pays you to go to the United States and stay there because of this social security tax payment.
If it is the law that the employer in the United States must pay the social security tax for his employees irrespective of citizenship, are they also going to accept paying the employers unemployment insurance tax of Canada? I am just trying to raise some of these things which are in my mind, and which I feel have to be answered before we can honestly give an answer to the resolution.
The principle, as I said, is of interest. Somehow we must find a way of taking care of these people. However, these ramifications are vital. I hope it will be possible to have some indication from the hon. member for Beauce or from the ministers concerned with the departments of labour and justice respectively as to what exactly would be involved in the acceptance of this motion. It is important to know, should we accept the motion in principle, what action we should have to take in amending our own act and in subsequent negotiations in order to bring about the best possible provisions for the benefit of our Canadian workers who are of necessity employed outside this country in the United States for two, three, four or five months of the year.
That is all I have to say. I think it was well worth while putting down the motion which stands in the name of the hon. member, and I look forward to the day when there will be in existence something which we should have had long ago; that is a form of international understanding or treaty between Canada and the United States providing for full protection of workers on both sides of the line.

speechtext:
In rising to speak on this resolution and to support the principle which it contains, I do so with some realization of the constitutional and practical aspects of the problem.
Any agreement involving international bodies raises its own particular difficulties. Although the resolution itself is very limited, the mover enlarged its scope, and I should like at this time to commend him for having done so. As Your Honour knows, the resolution deals only with woodsmen moving between Canada and the state of Maine, but the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Racine) in his remarks extended it to include New Hampshire. I think it should probably be extended further to apply to all Canadian labour enjoying benefits under the Unemployment Insurance Act of Canada.
Representing, as I do, the constituency of Charlotte, which contains the port of St. Stephen one of the border crossing points

to the United States, I may point out that we have a definite movement of labour through that port. I am not referring to those people who cross back and forth every day, or to those people who live in St. Stephen and work in Calais or in some other part of Maine. I am referring to movements which are more or less mass movements of labour through the ports of New Brunswick to the states of Maine and New Hampshire for various purposes, and for longer periods.
The hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) talked about the movement of certain classes of labour. He referred particularly to people going to the states of Maine and New Hampshire for the purpose of picking potatoes. I have obtained some figures dealing with this migration and although they are not too definite or too comprehensive I have been advised by government authorities that in 1959 we had 4,179 from the province of Quebec and 2,516 from the province of New Brunswick entering the state of Maine in connection with the potato harvest.
I realize that these people are not now covered by the provisions of the Canadian Unemployment Insurance Act. However, as the hon. member for Vancouver East has pointed out, there should possibly be an extension of the act to include these people. In the same year, 1959, 271 persons from the province of Quebec and 369 from New Brunswick entered the state of Maine for the purpose of harvesting fruit. I have also obtained from the Department of Labour the number of Canadian labourers from the provinces of Quebec and New Brunswick, and, possibly to a limited extent, from Nova Scotia, who were in the state of Maine at the end of each month during 1959. In January, there were 2,614; in February, 2,670; in March, 600; in April, 306; in May, 3,247; in June, 4,943; in July, 4,149; in August, 3,637; in September, 3,136; in October, 3,703; in November, 3,965; and in December, 3,729. You will see from the figures I have just given that there is a considerable mass movement of labour across the border in each and every month.
The hon. member for Victoria-Carleton (Mr. Montgomery) referred to some of the correspondence between this government and the governor of the state of New Hampshire, and pointed out on the basis of that correspondence that the state of New Hampshire does not at the present time have the necessary legislative power to enable it to enter into a reciprocity with the government of Canada. It is clear that enabling legislation must be passed, allowing this to be done. I think hon. members will find that the same situation exists as far as the state of Maine is concerned. The present reciprocal agreement between this
Unemployment Insurance government and the state of New York, dealing with insurance coverage for Canadian labourers provides that this government act only as an agency to collect from the employer in the state of New York the benefits which he should pay to his Canadian workers. I think a similar arrangement could be worked out as far as the state of Maine or the state of New Hampshire are concerned. This is a question of vital importance. Those people who leave our province-the province of New Brunswick-or my constituency in order to go to the state of Maine to obtain employment should receive the same benefits as those to which they would be entitled had they remained in Canada or, alternately, the same benefits as their co-workers on the United States side may receive.
There are things which must be worked out on an international basis, and they can only be worked out by labour, management and government working together. As was pointed out by the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton, this government has done some work in this field. I commend the hon. member for Beauce for having introduced this resolution and join with him in urging the government to try to enter into negotiations for a reciprocal agreement with the state of Maine and the state of New Hampshire not only for the purpose of covering woodsmen but for covering all Canadian labour now covered by our Unemployment Insurance Act and, if necessary, to have that act extended so that those people who go to the United States, especially from my constituency, at seasonal times should be properly covered.

Mr. Speaker, at this time I should like to say a few words on the resolution now before the house. First, I should like to compliment the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Racine) on introducing this resolution and giving the house and the country an opportunity to have up to date facts on this very important matter of coverage of unemployment insurance benefits for Canadian woodsmen working in the state of Maine.
The hon. member for Victoria-Carleton (Mr. Montgomery) said it was a subject which was not too well understood but on which much had been done in the past. I agree with the hon. member, and I also wish to join with him, and with the hon. member who has just taken his seat, in complimenting the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr), his department and the officials of the unemployment insurance office for trying to get an agreement with the state of Maine on this important matter.
The hon. member for Victoria-Carleton stated that the state of New Hampshire had no authority to sign such an agreement with
1072	HOUSE OF
Unemployment Insurance Canada. The important part of this motion deals with Canadian woodsmen working in the state of Maine. To emphasize the importance of this I should like to refer to a report presented to the meeting which was referred to, and which was held on September 22, 1959 in Boston, and which was composed of United States and Canadian representatives. In his report Mr. A. J. Corballis, acting deputy regional director, bureau of employment security, gave some very interesting figures for the year 1959. He said that the employment, by months, ranged from 306 in April, 1959 to 4,943 in June, 1959 and that the average employment during the 11-month period was 2,421. What is more interesting is the distribution by states of bonded woodsmen. One to 2 per cent were employed in New York; 5 per cent in Vermont; 5 per cent in New Hampshire; and 88 per cent to 90 per cent in the state of Maine. This shows that the main interest of Canadian woodsmen is definitely directed toward the state of Maine.
With regard to the question asked by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch), doubting the authority of the Canadian government to cover Canadian workers working on the American side, I would place on record again the statement made by the hon. member for Beauce when he said-and I shall quote in French:
(Translation):
The commission may, with the approval of the governor in council, make regulations to include in insurable employment any job outside Canada which, if it were done in Canada, would be insurable employment.
(Text):
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, this shows that the unemployment insurance commission has authority under its act to make regulations to cover Canadian woodsmen working outside of Canada. Furthermore, agreements have already been signed with all but four American states. This shows that some mutual arrangement could also be made with the state of Maine, if we would only come to a mutual understanding.
Reference was made to the conference on reciprocal agreements with Canada which took place on September 22, 1959. I hold in my hand a report of this conference. It states in part:
The principal objective of the conference was to explore the possibility of the employment security agencies of Maine and New Hampshire entering into reciprocal agreements with Canada to pay unemployment insurance benefits to Canadian workers released from employment in the United States. The meeting was chaired by Arthur C. Gernes, regional director of the bureau of employment security, United States department of labour, who had been asked at a previous meeting of the committee on imports of the American pulpwood industry to call together interested parties, including labour and management, to consider the subject. The Canadian government had on several 

occasions in the past expressed concern that no provision was being made in these two states for the reciprocal payment of unemployment insurance.
The Canadian delegation was represented by Mr. James McGregor, director of unemployment insurance of the unemployment insurance commission in Ottawa who, at the time, gave a detailed explanation of the Canadian commission's experience with unemployed woodsmen, and also by Mr. Alec Ouimet of the national employment service who, on that occasion, summarized the movement of Canadian woodsworkers in the United States.
The labour position was presented by Mr. Cecil Crawford, representative of the international brotherhood of pulp, sulphite and paper mill workers. In his brief he referred to the substantial membership of Canadian woodsworkers in local No. 809 who he said were acutely aware of the situation and joined with him in supporting the undertaking.
I also have the different reports which were presented at the meeting referred to. Mr. Ouimet in his brief said that Canadian workers are employed in the state of Maine for sap peeled wood from mid-May to midAugust, and again in the early fall to late February in other types of work. It shows that if Canada could come to a satisfactory agreement with the state of Maine the employment of a substantial number of Canadian workers would relieve the unemployment situation in Canada. In fact, during 1959 from 150 to 200 men were sent to work in the United States from the Woodstock office of the unemployment insurance commission; 400 were sent from Sherbrooke; 400 from Megantic; and as many as 4,500 to 5,000 from the Beauce area. It is also mentioned that one large Canadian contractor, operating in the state of Maine, has already got in touch with the New Brunswick minister af labour requesting that action be taken to make unemployment insurance benefits available for these men, as we were finding it more and more difficult to hire woodsworkers without having unemployment insurance coverage.
This might be the main reason for finding a solution to this important problem. I believe we have reached the point where the United States operators are finding it increasingly difficult to obtain Canadian woodsmen to work for them because of the lack of unemployment insurance coverage.
Mr. McGregor representing the unemployment insurance commission also gave a detailed report at the meeting to which reference has been made. He stated:
In lumbering and logging there is one economic area embracing parts of Quebec, New Brunswick, Maine, Vermont, New Hampshire and New York.

It is desirable that there should be as much freedom of movement as possible within this labour market area. The two chief legislative impediments are the immigration and unemployment insurance laws.
It was mentioned this afternoon by the mover of the resolution with respect to immigration that there is a standing quota permitted by the United States immigration law of 9,000 at the present time. In my opinion this quota is adequate to allow Canadian workers to obtain employment in the state of Maine. In his brief Mr. McGregor went on to state:
Discussion has been carried on over many years by Canada with both Maine and New Hampshire, by correspondence and also by discussion at the annual interstate benefit conference. In addition to correspondence between officers of the unemployment insurance commission and their opposite numbers in Maine and New Hampshire, there were exchanges in 1954 between labour minister Gregg and the governor of New Hampshire, and in 1958 between labour minister Starr and the governors of New Hampshire and Maine.
I may have understood the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton incorrectly but I thought I heard him say that negotiations were undertaken at the ministerial level only recently. The hon. member is shaking his head and if he did not say that I apologize.
I do not wish to be misunderstood.

maintopic: PROPOSED EXTENSION OF BENEFITS TO CANADIAN WOODSMEN IN STATE OF MAINE
speechtext:
I will accept the hon. member's word. Many solutions to this problem were suggested at the conference arising out of objections advanced by the representatives of the state of Maine. In my opinion agreement could easily be reached on many of the problems. The brief goes on to say:
Tentative proposals have been suggested along the following lines:
1. In the absence of any reciprocal agreement one suggested solution was that, as the problem is primarily one affecting Canada, the Canadian unemployment insurance provisions might be extended to permit a United States employer to insure Canadian woodsmen under the Canadian act while working in Maine or New Hampshire. This idea has not been seriously considered by Canada because in essence it means an extension of a piece of Canadian legislation to the territory of another country and this is open to objections that: (a) it might be contrary to international law.
In that respect I might say it is my belief that if an agreement could be signed with most of the states some solution acceptable to the state of Maine could be achieved. The brief continues:
(b) it would probably have to be on a voluntary basis at the option of the employer.
This is a possibility which in view of present conditions might satisfy the majority of the Canadian workers especially those employed in the state of Maine because there
Unemployment Insurance is now some question of the shortage of workers. United States operators are finding it difficult to obtain Canadian woodsmen because they cannot qualify for unemployment insurance benefits. Therefore there might be a possibility of the Canadian and United States authorities arriving at an agreement under which unemployment insurance contributions could be made on a voluntary basis at the option of the employer. The brief continues:
(d) it would not avoid duplication of contributions as Maine and New Hampshire would no doubt still require the employers to comply with their laws.
It seems to me that some solution could be found for this objection. Another suggestion which was tentatively considered by New Hampshire in 1951 was to have a reciprocal agreement accompanied by certain additional tests of availability.
The brief goes on to state:
It was felt that appropriate regulations within the spirit of article V of the reciprocal agreement between Canada and the United States could be made by Maine or New Hampshire to carry out the idea indicated above; i.e., to disqualify a migratory worker if he has, without good cause, refused an offer of suitable employment in the area of his previous employment in Maine or New Hampshire, distance alone being deemed not to be good cause. However, a change in the claimant's domestic or other circumstances since the time of his previous employment in the United States might constitute good cause for refusing employment so far removed from his home.
In concluding my remarks I wish to bring to the attention of the house an objection raised by the state of Maine to the effect that such a program would cost them a maximum of $1,500,000 a year. This objection does not seem to be borne out by the facts. It is estimated that it would actually cost between $100,000 and $240,000. The state of Vermont was taken as an indication of the cost. It cost that state $20,237 in 1957 for an average duration of benefits of seven and one half weeks.
With respect to possible administrative problems it was the concensus of the meeting that these would not be insurmountable and would not differ materially from those encountered in handling interstate claims with other states. I believe that this reveals that a solution is possible.
It was suggested by the hon. member for Beauce that the United States operators could have a Canadian representative in Canada who would hire the workmen for them and keep records of their employment with respect to salaries, contributions, etc. The Maine commission has indicated that it is extremely important that industry be assured of sufficient wood labour to supply its needs. This statement indicates that the

Unemployment Insurance United States operators are interested in securing Canadian woodsmen tor the industry.
As there are only four states of the union that do not have this reciprocal agreement with Canada now, it is a good indication of the progress that has been made in this field. As the end of the meeting which was held on September 22 last the chairman stated he would not hesitate to call another meeting of this group at any time in fulfilling his responsibilities as regional director of the bureau of employment security if he felt it would be of some value to get together again for a further examination of the situation.
We were given an opportunity of discussing this problem and we were given a chance to express our opinions. I feel that it would be a good suggestion to the Minister of Labour to call a similar conference at the first opportunity.
